summary: Discusses requirements for telepresence interoperability by describing behaviors and protocols for Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence (CLUE). It also covers the problem statement and definitions.

eli5.summary: Fancy video rooms use many cameras and screens at once. This lists what is needed so rooms from different makers can work together.

subtitle: What is needed for video rooms from different makers to talk to each other.

tldr.problem: Telepresence systems from different vendors do not interoperate because they describe and control video and audio streams differently, making multi-vendor conferences difficult or requiring expensive transcoding.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7262 specifies requirements for a protocol (CLUE) that lets telepresence endpoints exchange information about their camera and microphone arrangements, screen layouts, and capture characteristics so they can render remote sites correctly.
tldr.outcome: The CLUE protocol, defined in follow-on specifications, enables telepresence endpoints with different vendors' systems to negotiate and display video and audio in spatially correct ways.

today: RFC 7262 is an Informational RFC that defines requirements for the CLUE protocol. The CLUE protocol itself was subsequently specified in RFC 7875 and related documents, enabling telepresence systems to interoperate even when from different vendors.

sections.title: The Problem with Telepresence Interoperability
sections.content: Telepresence is a rich video conferencing experience designed to give participants a feeling of presence in the same room, achieved using high-fidelity audio and video. Unlike simple video calls, telepresence systems often use multiple cameras and screens at each site to capture and display natural-looking views of all participants. Each vendor has built their systems with different approaches: they use dissimilar techniques to describe and control multiple video streams, negotiate media characteristics differently, and often use proprietary protocol extensions beyond the standard Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). When trying to connect systems from different vendors, these differences create severe interoperability problems. Although some workaround is possible through transcoding and translation devices, these are expensive, often not fully automatic, and can introduce unwanted side effects like additional delay. The CLUE (Controlling Multiple Streams for Telepresence) work seeks to define a standard protocol that lets endpoints exchange information about their configuration, so they can adapt their behavior and provide a good user experience even when connected to different vendors' systems.
sections.eli5: When different video room makers try to connect, they often fail because they do things in completely different ways. This RFC is about what information rooms need to share so they can work together.

sections.title: How Telepresence Systems Work
sections.content: A telepresence system at a single site has multiple physical devices: cameras that capture video, microphones that capture audio, screens for displaying video, and loudspeakers for rendering audio. The problem arises because when Alice's endpoint sends video streams to Bob's endpoint, Bob needs to know which stream came from which camera and where that camera was positioned in Alice's room in order to render it correctly. If Alice's first stream is from her left camera but Bob assumes the first stream is from her right camera, Bob's display will be spatially inverted and confusing. Similarly, if Alice has three microphones arranged from left to right but Bob renders them in a different order, the audio will appear to come from the wrong direction. The RFC defines Endpoint Characteristics as the placement, angle, resolution, and mixing parameters of these devices. Each endpoint has a Layout describing how media streams are spatially arranged on its screens and speakers. For a multiparty conference, there may be a Multipoint Control Unit (MCU) that mixes and forwards media from multiple endpoints. CLUE enables endpoints to describe their characteristics and layouts, and to understand and adapt to those of the remote site.
sections.eli5: A room has cameras on the left, right, and maybe center, and speakers arranged the same way. When sending video to another room, you need to tell them which stream is from which camera so they can put it in the right place on their screens.

sections.title: Core Requirements for CLUE
sections.content: RFC 7262 enumerates 18 specific requirements for the CLUE solution. The most fundamental requirement is that the solution MUST support a description of the spatial arrangement of source video images that enables realistic reproduction at the receiver, including preservation of the left-right order and the up-down order of participants, plus the ability to identify the 3D location and coverage area of each capture. Similar requirements apply to audio: the solution MUST preserve spatial audio information so that Alice's voice appears to come from where she is actually sitting. The solution MUST also enable associations between audio and video (linking a speaker's voice to their video). It MUST support endpoints with different numbers of cameras, screens, microphones, and speakers; for example, one endpoint with 1 camera and 1 screen must be able to interoperate with another having 3 cameras and 3 screens. It MUST handle different video aspect ratios, display resolutions, and bit rates. It MUST ensure backward compatibility: endpoints that support CLUE extensions MUST still be able to set up a session with legacy endpoints that do not, using only standard SDP and SIP. Finally, it MUST support both point-to-point SIP sessions and SIP-based multipoint conferences, including both transcoding and switching approaches.
sections.eli5: The protocol needs to say where each camera and microphone is, match video to audio, handle rooms of different sizes, and still work with old video systems that do not understand the new protocol.

sections.title: Extensibility and Dynamic Behavior
sections.content: Telepresence systems are not static; endpoints may add or remove cameras and adjust their configurations during a call. RFC 7262 requires that any new specification for the solution MUST provide extensibility mechanisms so that future enhancements can be added without breaking existing implementations. The solution MUST support a mechanism for allowing information about media captures to change during a conference, enabling endpoints to advertise that they have reconfigured their camera layout or added a new display. Additionally, the solution MUST support mechanisms for secure exchange of capture information. The requirements apply to both point-to-point SIP sessions and multipoint conferences. The approach does not dictate telepresence architectural and implementation choices; vendors remain free to implement telepresence differently internally. CLUE simply describes a common protocol interface that allows different internal architectures to interoperate. Implementations are not mandated to use CLUE to describe their capabilities, nor required to act on received information, but those that do will provide a better user experience.
sections.eli5: The system needs to let rooms tell each other when they add a camera or change their setup during a call. It also needs to encrypt the message so snooping is not possible, and it needs to work with future improvements.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content: RFC 7262 covers several distinct use cases, all addressed to some degree by the CLUE requirements. Point-to-point meetings are the simplest: two sites with potentially different equipment need to agree on how to render each other's streams. Multipoint meetings involve three or more endpoints, and may include a centralized MCU that controls stream mixing and distribution. Heterogeneous systems are endpoints with wildly different numbers of cameras and screens; the protocol must enable graceful interoperation despite these differences. Presentation scenarios allow a participant to share slides or other content as an additional media stream, visible to all participants, possibly alongside the main telepresence feed. Related use cases are documented in RFC 7205. The requirements in RFC 7262 ensure that each of these scenarios is addressed and that interoperability can be achieved despite the diversity of telepresence systems deployed.
sections.eli5: The requirements cover simple two-room calls, big conference rooms with many sites, rooms that are very different sizes, and presentations shared during the call.
